title: What are the main garbage collectors — Serial GC (single-threaded, for small apps), Parallel GC (multi-threaded, Java 8 default, good throughput), G1 GC (Java 9+ default, region-based, targets low pause times), ZGC (ultra-low pause <10ms, Java 11+), Shenandoah (low pause, concurrent)?
shortTitle: What are the main garbage collectors?

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM ships with several garbage collectors, each making a different trade-off between pause time, throughput, and CPU usage. Serial GC uses a single thread and is suited to small applications. Parallel GC uses multiple threads to maximize throughput and was the Java 8 default. G1 GC divides the heap into regions and targets predictable low pause times, and it is the default from Java 9. ZGC and Shenandoah are concurrent collectors that keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds even on very large heaps.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India choosing how to clean its branches. Serial GC is one janitor cleaning the whole branch alone while everyone waits — fine for a tiny village branch. Parallel GC is a team of janitors cleaning together to finish fast, but customers still wait during the cleaning — great when you care most about total work done. G1 GC is a smart crew that cleans the dirtiest rooms first and promises the branch is never locked for more than a set number of minutes. ZGC and Shenandoah are an elite crew that cleans while customers keep transacting, so the branch barely pauses even if it is a huge headquarters.
s1_definition.oneliner: Serial for tiny apps, Parallel for throughput, G1 for balanced low pauses (the modern default), ZGC and Shenandoah for ultra-low pauses on huge heaps.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The JVM ships with several garbage collectors, each making a different trade-off between pause time, throughput, and CPU usage. Serial GC uses a single thread and is suited to small applications. Parallel GC uses multiple threads to maximize throughput and was the Java 8 default. G1 GC divides the heap into regions and targets predictable low pause times, and it is the default from Java 9. ZGC and Shenandoah are concurrent collectors that keep pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds even on very large heaps.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India choosing how to clean its branches. Serial GC is one janitor cleaning the whole branch alone while everyone waits — fine for a tiny village branch. Parallel GC is a team of janitors cleaning together to finish fast, but customers still wait during the cleaning — great when you care most about total work done. G1 GC is a smart crew that cleans the dirtiest rooms first and promises the branch is never locked for more than a set number of minutes. ZGC and Shenandoah are an elite crew that cleans while customers keep transacting, so the branch barely pauses even if it is a huge headquarters.

**One line to remember:** Serial for tiny apps, Parallel for throughput, G1 for balanced low pauses (the modern default), ZGC and Shenandoah for ultra-low pauses on huge heaps.

sections.s2_technical:
Serial GC uses a single thread for both Minor and Major collections and stops all application threads while it runs. Because it has no threading overhead, it is efficient for small heaps and single-core or constrained environments. You enable it with `-XX:+UseSerialGC`. It is a good fit for small command-line tools or tiny microservices with little memory.

Parallel GC, also called the throughput collector, uses multiple threads to perform Minor and Major collections faster, shortening the stop-the-world pauses compared to Serial. It optimizes for maximum throughput, meaning the application does the most useful work per unit of CPU, accepting that pauses can be longer when they do happen. It was the default up to Java 8 and you enable it with `-XX:+UseParallelGC`. It suits batch jobs and analytics where total completion time matters more than individual pause length.

G1 GC (Garbage First) is the default from Java 9. It divides the heap into many equal-sized regions rather than fixed Young and Old areas, and it collects the regions containing the most garbage first. It does much of its marking work concurrently and aims to meet a pause-time goal you set with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`. You enable it with `-XX:+UseG1GC`. It gives a good balance of throughput and predictable pauses, which is why it is the general-purpose default for most server applications.

ZGC and Shenandoah are low-latency collectors that do almost all their work concurrently with the application, including compaction, so pauses stay in the low single-digit milliseconds regardless of heap size, even hundreds of gigabytes. ZGC is enabled with `-XX:+UseZGC` and Shenandoah with `-XX:+UseShenandoahGC`. They trade a bit of throughput and extra CPU for extremely consistent, tiny pauses. A senior nuance: there is no universally best collector. You pick based on your service's priority — raw throughput, balanced behavior, or strict latency — and you validate the choice with GC logs and load testing rather than guessing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an overnight batch job that calculates interest on millions of accounts. Nobody is waiting on a screen; we just want it done as fast as possible. This is exactly where Parallel GC shines — it maximizes throughput and the occasional longer pause does not matter at 2 AM.

Problem 2 — The bank's main online API serves customers all day and must feel responsive, with no long freezes. This is exactly where G1 GC fits — balanced behavior with a pause-time target so customers never wait too long.

Problem 3 — The real-time trading engine must respond within a few milliseconds every single time, because a long GC pause during market hours could mean missed trades and lost money. This is exactly where ZGC or Shenandoah fit — concurrent collection keeps pauses tiny and consistent.

Our mini-project builds a `CollectorDemo` that detects which collector the JVM is currently using (via `GarbageCollectorMXBean`), runs an identical workload, and reports pause behavior. A `WorkloadRunner` simulates account interest calculation so the reader can run it under different `-XX:+Use...GC` flags and compare the GC logs.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
jvm-collectors-demo/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/jvm/
            ├── CollectorDemo.java         (main runnable demo)
            ├── Account.java               (account with balance)
            ├── WorkloadRunner.java        (interest calc workload)
            └── CollectorInfo.java         (reports active collector)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/jvm/*.java

# Run with Parallel GC (throughput — good for overnight batch)
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.CollectorDemo

# Run with G1 GC (balanced low pause — good for online API)
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.CollectorDemo

# Run with ZGC (ultra-low pause — good for trading engine)
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xlog:gc \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.jvm.CollectorDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million accounts, each with a balance and a 6.5% annual interest rate; the JVM launched under a chosen collector flag.

Step 1 — The JVM starts with the selected collector. `CollectorInfo.printActiveCollector()` reads `GarbageCollectorMXBean` names. For Parallel GC it shows "PS Scavenge, PS MarkSweep"; for G1 it shows "G1 Young Generation, G1 Old Generation"; for ZGC it shows "ZGC Cycles, ZGC Pauses".

Step 2 — The workload begins. For each of the million accounts, a new Account object and a few BigDecimal objects are created in Eden. The allocation rate is very high.

Step 3 — Eden fills repeatedly. The active collector performs Minor collections. Under Parallel GC, multiple threads do this fast but with stop-the-world pauses. Under G1, collections honor the 100ms pause target. Under ZGC, collection runs concurrently and pauses stay around 1ms.

Step 4 — The daily interest for each account is computed and summed into a running BigDecimal total. The old Account objects become unreachable immediately and are reclaimed on the next collection.

Step 5 — After the loop, the total interest is logged. Then `printGcStats()` reports how many collections happened and the total pause time, which differs sharply by collector.

Final output (G1 run):

```
2026-10-31 22:58:00 [INFO] Active GC collector(s): G1 Young Generation, G1 Old Generation
2026-10-31 22:58:03 [INFO] Total interest accrued across accounts: 89041095.20
2026-10-31 22:58:03 [INFO] Collector G1 Young Generation      collections=73 totalPause=142ms
2026-10-31 22:58:03 [INFO] Collector G1 Old Generation        collections=0  totalPause=0ms
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```

    │
    ▼
  WorkloadRunner.calculateDailyInterest(1,000,000)
    │ new Account + BigDecimal ×millions
    ▼
  Eden fills ──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
    │                      │              │              │
    ▼ SerialGC             ▼ ParallelGC   ▼ G1GC          ▼ ZGC/Shenandoah
  1 thread STW          N threads STW   regions, pause   concurrent compaction
  long pause            fast but STW    target ~100ms    pause ~1ms
    │                      │              │              │
    └──────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
                  CollectorInfo.printGcStats()
                  collections count + total pause time
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM offers several garbage collectors, and each one makes a different trade-off between pause time, throughput, and CPU cost. Serial GC uses a single thread and stops the whole application while it collects, which is perfectly fine for small applications and constrained environments. Parallel GC, which was the default up to Java 8, uses many threads to collect quickly and is tuned for maximum throughput, so it suits batch and analytics workloads where total completion time matters more than any single pause. G1 GC, the default from Java 9 onward, splits the heap into many regions, collects the ones with the most garbage first, and lets you set a target maximum pause time, giving a balanced behavior that fits most server applications. ZGC and Shenandoah go further by doing almost all their work, including compaction, concurrently with the application, keeping pauses in the low single-digit milliseconds even on very large heaps.

The key insight I always bring up is that there is no single best collector. The right choice depends entirely on what the service cares about most. If it is raw throughput on a batch job, Parallel GC. If it is balanced, predictable behavior for a general online service, G1. If it is strict, consistent low latency for something like real-time trading, ZGC or Shenandoah. And you never choose by intuition alone; you validate with GC logs and load tests.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, we use exactly this split. Our overnight interest calculation batch runs under Parallel GC because nobody is waiting and we just want it finished fast. Our main customer-facing API runs under G1 with a pause-time target so the application never freezes long enough for a customer to notice. And our real-time trading engine runs under ZGC, because during market hours a long GC pause could mean a missed trade and real financial loss, so we accept a little extra CPU usage in exchange for pauses that stay around a millisecond every single time. Choosing the collector deliberately for each workload is one of the most impactful tuning decisions I make.

---

keyPoints: Serial: single-thread, small heaps, client apps
G1 (default since Java 9): region-based, predictable pauses
